text.hook:
Memory ordering is where C++ interview answers get vague fastest.

Here is the mental model, plus the 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it for your next interview. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The two questions every atomic answers
2. The three layers you must never mix
3. The happens-before chain to say out loud
4. Why "thread 1 ran first" proves nothing
5. The exact definition of a data race
6. Six myths, busted (slides 7-8)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: what happens with `flag.store(true, std::memory_order_acquire)`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Undefined behaviour: acquire is not a valid order for a store (precondition violation). GCC and Clang compile it silently; `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` aborts.

slides.lead: What interviewers are actually checking for, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: Every atomic operation answers two separate questions

cards.label: Atomicity
cards.text: Can threads touch *this variable* without races, torn values or lost updates?

cards.label: Ordering
cards.text: What does it guarantee about *other* memory around it?

slides.takeaway: Atomicity is always there, even with `relaxed`. The memory order only changes the ordering answer.

slides.title: Never mix these in one answer
rows: instruction selection, compiler reordering, compiler barriers
slides.takeaway: Answer at the C++ level first. Hardware is one possible implementation.

slides.lead: Execution order is not synchronization. Only a happens-before edge makes the later read safe.

slides.title: The standard's definition
slides.warn: Result: undefined behaviour for the whole program, not "a stale value".

items.myth: "Release flushes the store buffer. Acquire invalidates the cache."
items.truth: Possible hardware effects. The C++ guarantee is a synchronizes-with edge when the acquire reads the released value.
Acquire never waits. A load that runs first just reads the old value and synchronizes with nothing.
Relaxed is still fully atomic. It is exactly right for counters and flags that publish nothing.
It constrains which outcomes are allowed, not scheduling.

items.myth: "Any memory barrier makes the code correct."
items.truth: You need a matched pair: release side and acquire side, on the same atomic object.

items.myth: "volatile is fine for a flag between threads."
items.truth: volatile gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering. Use std::atomic.

slides.hero:
Atomic:
"this operation is safe."

Memory order:
"how it relates to everything else."
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The consumer was "fixed" to use memory_order_acquire.
The producer was left alone. 🧵

Is it thread-safe now?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This is the most common half-fix in memory ordering code reviews. Look at both sides before you answer.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: fix it with fences instead. Does `atomic_thread_fence(release)` go before or after `ready.store(true, relaxed)`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Before the store. A release fence placed after the publishing store lets `payload = 500` still be reordered after the flag.

slides.title:
The consumer now uses acquire.
Thread-safe?

bullets: An acquire load synchronizes-with a **release** store whose value it reads.
A relaxed store has no release semantics: no happens-before edge.
So `payload = 500` and the read race: UB for the whole program.
"The producer probably runs first" is irrelevant. Execution order is not synchronization.

slides.title: Release and acquire are a pair
bullets: Half-fix: relaxed gives acquire nothing to pair with.
The release store synchronizes-with the acquire load that reads `true`.
So the write happens-before the read: always 500.
slides.takeaway: Release on the store, acquire on the load.

text.hook:
Everything is memory_order_relaxed.
One writer stores 10 then 20. One reader loads twice. 🧵

Which outputs are possible?
Lock in your picks below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: "Relaxed means anything goes" is the answer that fails here. Slide 3 shows where relaxed really does surprise you.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: a shared_ptr-style reference count. Which memory order does the increment need, and which does the decrement need? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Increment: relaxed (you already hold a reference, so the object cannot die). Decrement: release, plus acquire in the thread that reaches zero before `delete`: `fetch_sub(1, acq_rel)`.

slides.title:
All relaxed. Which `a b`
outputs are possible?
slides.cta: Pick all that apply, then swipe ➜

slides.verdict_sub: "20 10" and "10 0" are impossible, even with relaxed
bullets: Modification order of `x`: `0 → 10 → 20` (same thread, so sequenced-before fixes it).
Read-read coherence: once a thread has read a value, a later load of the **same** object cannot return an older one.

slides.title: One atomic vs two atomics
bullets: Each atomic has its own modification order. Nothing links `x` and `y`.
No data race: the stale `0` is a defined value, just unwanted. Publishing `x` through a flag `y` needs release/acquire.
slides.takeaway: One modification order **per object**: relaxed keeps per-object coherence, not cross-object order.

text.hook:
Two threads. Two flags. Four possible outputs.
Only some of them can actually happen. 🧵

Lock in your picks below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This is the classic store-buffering (Dekker) test. Slide 3 shows why one small change in memory order changes the answer.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: if only Thread 1 uses release/acquire and Thread 2 stays seq_cst, is "nothing" possible? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Yes. The single total order covers only seq_cst operations. Weakening one side's operations brings the "nothing printed" outcome back.

slides.title:
Two threads, two flags.
Which outputs are possible?
slides.cta: Pick all that apply, then swipe ➜

bullets: Nothing printed would need both loads to read `false`.
Then each load comes before the other thread's store in the single seq_cst order.
With program order that forms a **cycle**. Impossible.
"T1 T2" is fine: `x.store, y.store, y.load, x.load`.
slides.cta: Now change it to release / acquire ➜

slides.title: Same code, weaker ordering
slides.takeaway: Store then load on two different variables (Dekker pattern) needs seq_cst. Release/acquire does not forbid it.

text.hook:
T1 writes config and releases `a`. T3 only ever acquires `b`.
"T3 never synchronized with T1, so it races." Agree?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Three threads, two flags, one plain std::string. The rule that decides it also makes every pipeline work.

slides.title:
T3 never touches `a`.
Is reading `config` safe?
options: Safe only if all are seq_cst

slides.verdict_sub: happens-before is transitive. GCC 11 + TSan: no race reported
bullets: T1: write `config`, then release `a`.
T2's acquire of `a` syncs with it. T2 then releases `b`.
T3's acquire of `b` syncs with T2. Chain: write → T3's read.
Each pipeline stage syncs only with the previous one, yet sees all earlier writes.
slides.wrong: "T3 must also acquire `a` to see T1's data"

slides.title: T2 stores `b` relaxed
bullets: A relaxed store releases nothing, so T3's acquire syncs with nobody.
Same break if T2 stored `b` before acquiring `a`.
slides.takeaway: Happens-before chains across any number of threads, if every link is a real release/acquire pair.

text.hook:
"Release works because it flushes the store buffer."
An interviewer said this. Sounds senior. Is it right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The best answer here is about layers, not about hardware.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: on x86-64 with GCC, what does a seq_cst `store` compile to, and why is it the costly one? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `xchg` (implicitly locked): a full barrier that drains the store buffer. Release and relaxed stores are a plain `mov`.

slides.title: x86-64, GCC `-O2`. What does the release store compile to?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11 `-O2`: `movb $1, ready(%rip)`. No flush at all.
bullets: C++ defines release by happens-before: if the acquire reads `true`, `payload == 42` holds.
x86 is TSO: stores already stay in order. On ARMv8 a release store is `stlr`.
Coherence (MESI) alone gives no ordering: a core can still delay stores in a store buffer.
Answer in 3 layers: C++, compiler, hardware. Go to hardware only if asked.

slides.title: The costly store is seq_cst
slides.takeaway: Define release/acquire with happens-before. Store buffers and MESI are implementation details (x86-64, GCC).
